New Specialization Proposal Walkthrough
New Specialization Proposal Walkthrough
This guide provides step-by-step procedural instructions for completing and submitting a New Specialization Proposal in Kuali. It focuses on navigating the form, including what to select or enter in each field.
*In Kuali, Specializations are also known as Sub-plans, Options, Tracks, and Concentrations.
The guide is organized by proposal section (panel), so you can jump directly to a section when you need help.
This guide does not provide guidance on course content or academic decisions. Consult your department and applicable curriculum committees for questions about developing the course itself.
Navigate by Section
Related toolkit entry: Specialization Modification Proposal Walkthrough

Familiarize yourself with URI’s curricular process before beginning your proposal. This will help you understand the steps involved in the curricular process and accurately estimate how long your proposal may take to reach approval.
How the Curriculum Process Works
Related toolkit entry: How the Curriculum Process Works
Approval Calendar
Related toolkit entry: Approval Calendar

You will need access to Kuali Curriculum Management (Kuali CM) to propose any curricular item.
Kuali Basics
Related toolkit entry: Kuali Basics

From your browser, navigate to Kuali Curriculum Management (CM).
Select Curriculum to open your Dashboard .
Related toolkit entry: Dashboard
From the left-hand navigation menu, select Specializations.
On the Programs page, select + New Specialization in the upper-right corner.
The following sections of this walkthrough are grouped by section of the proposal form.

Complete the following fields with your contact information.
Proposer Name Your name is automatically populated based on your Kuali account.
Proposer Title Enter your university role.
Proposer Email Enter your URI email address. This is the email reviewers will use if they have questions about your proposal.
Additional Proposer(s) Use this section to identify additional individuals who can speak to the proposed program. Individuals listed here will not receive Kuali notifications or have access to edit the proposal. Their inclusion simply provides transparency to the reviewing committees about who else is involved in or can speak to the proposal.
Inherit From Begin typing the name of the parent program, then select the program from the list.

Effective Term & Year Select the term and year in which you intend the specialization to become effective. If the selected effective term has passed the applicable deadline by the time the proposal reaches the Faculty Senate, it will automatically be updated to the next available term.
First Graduation Term Select the term and year in which you anticipate the first students will graduate with this credential.
Level Select the level of the specialization: Undergraduate, Graduate, or Dual Dual applies to ABMs and 4+1 specializations.
🔽 The following field will appear only if Dual is chosen for Level.
Dual Type Refer to the linked pages above to understand the difference between ABMs & 4+1s
Academic Calendar Select the academic calendar for the specialization: Accelerated 7-week through URI Online, or Traditional 14-week with Summer and J-Term Sessions (must coincide with parent program).
College Select the college in which the program is housed.
Department Select the department in which the program is housed.

Is this interdisciplinary? The intent of this question is to identify whether the parent program of this specialization is jointly owned by multiple academic departments. If yes, the percentage of ownership assigned to each department must be provided in the curriculum worksheet.
🔽 The following field will appear only if “Yes” is chosen for Is this interdisciplinary?
Additional Department(s) and College(s) Enter departments sharing ownership of this program.
Academic Specialization Title Enter the title of the specialization. See the linked page for title formatting guidelines.
Specialization Description List the requirements of the specialization. Only specialization-specific requirements should be listed here, and no program requirements should be duplicated.
Admission Requirements If the specialization has specific admission requirements, list them here. Otherwise, enter: “See admission requirements for {Program Title}.”
Total specialization credits (excluding program credits) Enter the number of credits required for this specialization.
🔽 The following field will appear only if ABM is chosen for Dual Type

Total double-counted course credits Enter the number of credits double counted towards this ABM.
Attach Curriculum Worksheet
Upload a curriculum worksheet outlining the courses, credits, and other requirements that make up the proposed specialization’s curriculum within its parent program. You may use the University’s standard curriculum worksheets, or you may clearly include all requirements in a word document or PDF.

🔽 This section will only appear if the Dual Type is ABM.
Answer the following prompts:
List all bachelor’s degrees and majors eligible for application to this ABM program. Include any specializations (sub-plans or tracks).
Total earned credits at the time of ABM application (minimum 75)
Total earned credits required for admission (minimum 90)
Courses Approved for Double Counting

New Temporary & Permanent Course Email
Date: May 31, 2027 (2027-05-31)
Tags: Temp Course Email
New Temporary & Permanent Course Email
The New Temporary & Permanent Course Email is distributed to all faculty, deans, and associate and assistant deans on the last weekday of each month. Recipients then have seven days to submit comments to the CASC Chair, GEC Chair, or Dean of the Graduate School regarding any potential or perceived content overlap involving a new temporary or permanent course.
The email serves two purposes:
Provides notice of upcoming Faculty Senate review. Courses included in the email have already been reviewed and approved by their respective College Curriculum Committees and will next be reviewed by the appropriate Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee: CASC, GEC, or Graduate Council.
Provides an opportunity to identify potential content overlap. College Curriculum Committees may review the courses included in the email to identify any potential or perceived overlap with courses offered or proposed by other colleges. Any concerns can then be raised before the courses proceed to Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee review.

Credential Type
Tags: programs
Short Description: Identifies the type of academic credential awarded for a program. (Degree, Major, Minor, Certificate)
Credential Type

The degree is the academic credential awarded by the University upon successful completion of an approved program of study and its associated requirements. Degrees may include bachelor's, master's, and doctoral degrees.
The major is the primary field of study within a degree program, consisting of a defined set of courses and requirements that students must complete.
University Manual 8.20.40 Major Fields of Study. An undergraduate student’s concentrated field of study in a degree-granting college shall be the student’s “major”; Fannon Institute students may have a “preferred major.” The major field of study for graduate students shall be the student’s “program.”

Undergraduate programs are required to have a minimum or 120 credits, and a maximum of 148 (UM 8.21.10)
Undergraduate programs shall include at least 6 credits of free electives (UM 8.21.10)
General Education requirements shall apply to all undergraduate programs (UM 8.21.11)
A cumulative average of at least 2.00 is required to graduate from all undergraduate degrees. (UM 8.22.10)
Master’s degree programs with thesis require a minimum of 30 credits. 18 must be from content-based courses, 6 must be thesis courses. (GSM 7.44.1)
Master’s degree programs without thesis require a minimum of 30 credits. (GSM 7.45.1)
Doctoral students must complete a Program of Study with a minimum of 64 credit hours beyond the undergraduate degree (GSM 7.54) (See GSM sections 7.54 and 7.21)
In Kuali, the term program refers to all credential types; Degrees, majors, minors, and certificates. In the Manual, program refers to a graduate student’s major field of study.

A secondary concentration of undergraduate courses that provides students with a defined area of study outside their major. A minor generally requires 18 or more credits and is listed on the student’s permanent academic record after graduation.
University Manual 8.20.50 Minor Fields of Study. Undergraduate Students may declare a “minor” field of study. A minor is a secondary concentration of courses.

18 or more credits of related studies offered by one or more departments or programs and sponsored by a faculty member. (UM 8.20.50)
At least 12 credits at the 200-level or above ( UM 8.20.51)
At least 8 credits must be earned at URI (UM 8.20.51)
Minimum GPA average of 2.0 must be earned in the minor’s required courses (UM 8.20.51)
A maximum of two courses can apply to both the major and minor field of study (UM 8.20.52)
An approved course of study designed to further knowledge in a field of interest, provide specialized training, and/or enhance professional skills.

Undergraduate certificates generally require 15-21 credits of coursework (UM 8.20.70)
Undergraduate certificates are available to degree seeking and certificate-only seeking undergraduate students (UM 8.20.70)
Undergraduate certificate courses may not be pass/fail (UM 8.20.71)
Graduate certificates require 12 credits minimum, 16 credits maximum. (GSM Appendix J.1.1)
Post-master’s graduate certificates require 12 credits minimum, 18 credits maximum. (GSM Appendix J.1.1)

Instructional Delivery Method
Tags: courses
Short Description: The instructional delivery method. Also known as "method of instruction.”
Instructional Delivery Method
Provided below is the complete list of approved methods of instruction, as proposed in FSEC Report #2024-2025-03 and subsequently approved by the Faculty Senate through Bill #24-25-12 on January 23, 2025.
A course in which the primary method is presentation and students are expected to participate in a variety of ways, such as small-group discussions, questions and answers, writing-exercises, etc.
Applied course work, generally involving experimentation or observation, typically using special equipment (including computers and specialized software).
Separate sections of a lecture course regularly scheduled for discussion.
Supervised work with an emphasis on performance and creativity in which faculty instruct, assist, and critique.
Course offered to a small group (usually no more than 20 students) where participants actively exchange ideas and findings based on readings or research.

One-on-one instruction in which the student enters into an agreement with the instructor that defines the focus of inquiry and nature of activities. Includes tutorials, directed readings, special projects.
Structured experiences where the primary aim is to connect theory with practice. Includes clinics, internships, externships, student teaching, field experiences. May include regular class meetings.
Similar to a seminar, with emphasis on applied rather than theoretical learning, but not offered for degree-program credit.
